function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script) to finish the task.  
I’ve also included the exact contents of the three new files that will be added to the repo:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight container for the Node.js app |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deployment + Service definition for Kubernetes |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | GitHub Actions workflow that builds & pushes the image on every push to `main` |

> **NOTE** – The repo you mentioned (`git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`) is assumed to contain a standard Node.js project with an `app.js` (or similar) that listens on port `3000`. If the actual entry point or port differs, adjust the files accordingly.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the Repository

```bash
# Make sure you have SSH keys set up for GitHub
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse & Create Files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` at the root of the repo:

```dockerfile
# Use official Node.js LTS image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is small and includes only the essentials.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a clean install from `package-lock.json`.  
> * The app is started with `node app.js` – change if your entry point differs.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a directory `k8s` and inside it a file `deployment.yaml`:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # Adjust if you use another registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deploys 2 replicas of the container.  
> * Exposes the app via a `ClusterIP` service on port 80 (internally forwards to 3000).  
> * Uses the image `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest`; replace with your own registry if needed.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions Workflow

Create the directory `.github/workflows` (if it doesn’t exist) and add `ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          file: ./Dockerfile
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest
```

> **How it works**  
> * Triggers on every push to `main`.  
> * Builds the Docker image using the Dockerfile.  
> * Pushes the image to GitHub Container Registry (`ghcr.io`).  
> * Uses the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN` for authentication – no extra secrets required.

---

## 3️⃣ Add All Changed Files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

---

### 🎉 Done!

You now have:

* A Dockerfile that builds a minimal image for your Node.js app.  
* Kubernetes deployment & service YAMLs ready for `kubectl apply -f k8s/`.  
* A GitHub Actions workflow that automatically builds & pushes the image whenever you push to `main`.

Feel free to tweak the image names, tags, or registry as per your organization’s conventions. Happy coding!
